source_title: Premium: Venture Capital Is Killing Itself
other_side: Zitron argues that the 2012 JOBS Act let companies stay private for so long that most of the growth is priced in before the public can buy, so IPOs mainly let early investors sell. He says Anthropic's reported two trillion dollar valuation rests on projected annual revenue of 200 billion dollars and a 30 trillion dollar market, and calls the AI boom "the largest valuation bubble in the history of technology". Only the opening part of the piece is free to read, so the proposed remedies are not covered here.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is who ends up owning, and being paid by, AI's upside. Both accept as fact that Anthropic is heading for a public listing at a valuation above a trillion dollars, that private markets set the price until now, and that a small group of founders and early investors hold much of the value. The empirical question is whether public investors earn a return after listing; the observable is how Anthropic and SpaceX shares trade against their issue prices over the following year. The residue is worldview: whether a company growing this fast should be judged on projected markets or on audited results. For Whittemore to be vindicated, wealth must be shared by choice, through funds or distributions, before governments force it. For Zitron, listings must prove to be exits for insiders and later buyers must lose money. Both are polemicists with incentives, Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron certain of a bubble and anti-hype. The signal is that both think current ownership is too concentrated. Watch how the stock behaves after the Anthropic listing.
